chapter.title: Stations and the belt

cards.body:
Double-click any box in n8n after a run, and it shows you exactly what it just handed to the next box. That is most of this chapter.

On your assembly line, each box is a **station that does one job**. The belt between stations carries small packets, and each packet has labelled parts.
cards.simpler: In n8n, after a run, double-click any box. It shows you exactly what that box just passed to the next one. That is most of this chapter. Think of your setup as an assembly line. Each box is a **station that does one job**. A belt runs between the stations and carries small packets. Each packet has parts, and each part has a label.

cards.prompt: A coffee line: the bell rings when an order comes in. Station 1 writes a slip with two parts: drink is 'flat white', name is 'Ana'. Station 2 prints the cup label. What does station 2 work from?

options.text: The slip station 1 just put on the belt
The bell, which it asks again for the order details
Every slip the line has ever made

whyNot.b: That's the trigger, not the belt: the bell only starts the line. It carries nothing down it.
whyNot.c: That's a filing cabinet, not a belt: a station works from this run's packets, not old ones.

cards.reteach: Think of a relay race. Each runner takes the baton from the runner right before them. By default, each box works from what the box right before it passed on.

cards.title: Stations are nodes, packets are items
cards.body:
Every box on the n8n canvas is a *node*, a station that does one job: wait for the bell, tidy some text, send a message.

**Each node hands its work to the next as items.** An *item* is one packet, like one order slip. Inside it are *fields*, named parts that each hold a value: name is Ana, drink is flat white. Twenty form replies become twenty items.

You'd think you have to guess what's on the belt. You never do. After a run, double-click a node. The *output panel* on the right shows what it passed on, with the number of items at the top.
cards.simpler: Each box in n8n is a node: a station that does one job, like sending a message. **Each node passes its work to the next as items.** An item is one packet, like one order slip. Inside are fields, labelled parts that each hold a value: name is Ana, drink is flat white. Twenty form replies make twenty items. After a run, double-click a node. The output panel shows what it passed on, and how many items.

cards.title: Leila's Monday line
cards.body: Leila wants a reminder every Monday at 9:00 to send invoices. Station 1 is a Schedule Trigger, and its output panel shows 1 item holding the date and time it fired. Station 2 is an Edit Fields node, which lets you type in named parts by hand: task is 'send invoices', owner is 'Leila'. Its panel now reads 1 item with two fields, **task and owner**. Before she builds station 3, Leila already knows exactly what it will receive.
cards.simpler: Leila wants a reminder every Monday at 9:00 to send invoices. Station 1 is a Schedule Trigger. Its output panel shows 1 item, holding the date and time it went off. Station 2 is an Edit Fields node, where you type in labelled parts yourself: task is 'send invoices', owner is 'Leila'. Now its panel shows 1 item with two fields, **task and owner**. Before building station 3, Leila already knows what it will get.

cards.prompt: Your third node sends a message, but there's a blank where the task should be. Where do you look first?

options.text: The output panel of node 2, to see what it actually handed on
Delete node 3 and build it again

whyNot.a: That's the bell, not the belt: when it rings has nothing to do with what's inside the packet.
whyNot.c: That's a rebuild, not a check: a new node would receive the same packet and leave the same blank.

cards.reteach: When a station does something odd, the cause is usually in what it was handed. Open the node before it and read its output panel. Every field and its exact name is listed there. Fix the packet, and the next station gets it right.

cards.title: One job, once per item
cards.body:
Here's the part that surprises people. **A station does its job once for every item it receives.** Hand a message node 1 item and it sends 1 message. Hand it 30 and it sends 30.

Most days, that's exactly what you want. Thirty new sign-ups get thirty welcome emails, and you never have to say 'repeat'. The packets roll past one after another, like parcels past a packing table.

So the item count at the top of the output panel matters as much as the fields. '30 items' means the next station is about to work 30 times.
cards.simpler: This part surprises people. **A station does its job once for every item it gets.** Give a message node 1 item and it sends 1 message. Give it 30 and it sends 30. Usually that's what you want. Thirty sign-ups get thirty welcome emails, and you never have to say 'repeat'. It's like parcels rolling past a packing table. So watch the item count in the output panel. '30 items' means the next station will work 30 times.

cards.body: Tom tested his new line on a list of 40 colleagues, with the message station pointed at his own Slack to be safe. He clicked run, and his phone buzzed 40 times while he was still reading the first message. He'd expected one message listing everyone. The clue was already on screen: '40 items' in the output panel of the station before.
cards.simpler: Tom tested his new workflow on a list of 40 coworkers. To be safe, he pointed the message station at his own Slack. He clicked run, and his phone buzzed 40 times while he was still reading the first message. He had expected one message listing everyone. The warning sign was already on screen: **'40 items'** in the output panel of the station before.

cards.prompt: An Edit Fields node shows '12 items' in its output panel. The next station sends an email. You click run. What happens?

options.text: Nothing, because an email node only accepts 1 item

whyNot.a: That's one packet, not twelve: the 12 items would have to be packed into 1 before you'd get a single email.
whyNot.b: That's a limit email nodes don't have: by default, a station works through every item it's handed.

cards.reteach: By default, the belt doesn't bundle packets together. Each item rolls past the station on its own, and the station does its one job on each. Twelve items in means twelve jobs done.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Each box in n8n is a station that does one job and passes its work down the belt as items, packets of named fields. Open the output panel to see exactly what a station handed on and how many items, because the next station acts once per item.

Tomorrow: plugging in your real work apps, so a station can act as you.
cards.simpler: Each box in n8n is a station that does one job. It passes its work down the belt as items, which are packets of labelled fields. Open the output panel to see exactly what a station passed on, and how many items. That count matters, because **the next station works once per item**. Tomorrow, you'll plug in your real work apps, so a station can act as you.

cards.body: Open last chapter's workflow. Add an Edit Fields node right after the Schedule Trigger, with one field called task, set to anything. Run it, double-click the node, and read the output panel. Count the items.
cards.simpler: Open the workflow from last chapter. Right after the Schedule Trigger, add an Edit Fields node. Give it one field called task, and set it to anything you like. Run the workflow. Then double-click the Edit Fields node and read its output panel. **Count the items** it passed on.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now connect three nodes in a row and read exactly what each station hands to the next.

dubious_claims: 'a station only sees what the station before it just handed over' (card 2, feedback for c): false, because an n8n node can read any earlier node's output, for example with $('Node name').
'each box gets exactly what the box before it passed on, nothing more' (card 2, reteach): the same overstatement.

'a station takes any number of items and works through each one' (card 8): mostly true, but nodes have an 'Execute Once' setting and some nodes, like Aggregate, combine items. 'Any' and 'each' are too absolute.
repairedFrom.why: Card 2's feedback and reteach say a node gets what the node before it passed on, 'nothing more', and 'only sees' that packet. That is false in n8n, where a node can pull data from any earlier node, so readers learn a wrong rule that will trip them up later.
repairedFrom.fix: In card 2, change the whyNot for c to 'That's a filing cabinet, not a belt: a station works from this run's packets, not old ones.' and change the reteach to 'By default, each box works from what the box right before it passed on.'
